meta.note: Every quote was machine-checked as a contiguous substring of the saved source text (comparison ignores whitespace/punctuation; inline reference numbers removed only where the quote stops before them; table quotes have " / " cell separators added). read_level says how much of each source was read. license is as stated in the article XML; abstract-only sources were not licence-checked.

claims.statement: The annular pulleys hold the finger flexor tendons against the phalanges and prevent the tendons from lifting away from the bone (bowstringing) during finger flexion.
claims.quote: These ligaments prevent bowstringing of the flexor tendons, i.e. distancing of the tendons from the phalanges during flexion of the finger.
claims.cited_reference: No citation attached to this sentence in the source (general anatomy statement).

claims.statement: The A2 pulley is described as the thickest and strongest of the five annular pulleys.
claims.cited_reference: Berrigan ref 1: Smith J, Rizzo M, Lai JK. J Ultrasound Med 2010;29:1531-1542 (not checked).

claims.statement: The finger flexor pulley system is described as five annular (A1-A5) and three cruciate (C1-C3) pulleys, with A2 and A4 the strongest; one review instead counts four cruciate pulleys (see notes).
claims.quote: five annular ligaments/pulleys (A1-5, listed from proximal to distal) and three cruciate ligaments/pulleys (C1-3, listed from proximal to distal)
claims.cited_reference: Sentence on A2/A4 strength cites Larsson ref 5: Crowley TP. J Hand Microsurg 2012;4:25-29 (abstract only seen).

claims.statement: Loss of one or more pulleys increases the tendon-to-bone distance (bowstringing), with loss of strength and reduced range of motion.
claims.cited_reference: Simon ref 9: Schoffl V, Hochholzer T, El-Sheikh Y, Lutter C. Hand and fingers. In: Climbing Medicine. Springer; 2021:55-94 (book chapter, not read).

claims.statement: Pulley injuries are described on a spectrum from strain through partial tear and complete single tear to multiple-pulley tears.
claims.cited_reference: Simon ref 3: Lutter C, Tischer T, Schoffl VR. Br J Sports Med 2021;55:857-864 (abstract only seen; the abstract does not contain the grading).

claims.statement: A2 pulley tears may present acutely or chronically and range from small partial tears to large complete tears.
Pulley injuries can arise from a single high-intensity overload or from persistent overuse.
claims.quote: Injuries to the annular ligaments, i.e. pulley-injuries, can be both acute, e.g. during a single high intensity overload, or as a result of continued persistent overuse [11].
claims.cited_reference: Larsson ref 11: Schoffl V et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2003;14(2):94-100.

claims.statement: Significant A2 pulley injury allows bowstringing, which can lead to loss of range of motion and reduced finger function.
claims.cited_reference: Following sentence cites Berrigan ref 2: Heithoff SJ et al. J Hand Surg Am 1988;13:567-570 (not checked).

claims.statement: A review reports that the crimp grip places about 36 times more force on the A2 pulley than a slope (open) grip.
claims.cited_reference: Berrigan ref 12: Vigouroux L et al. J Biomech 2006;39:2583-2592 (abstract checked: see next claim).

claims.statement: A biomechanical model study estimated A2 pulley force to be 36 times lower in the slope grip than in the crimp grip (A4: 4 times lower).
A cadaver loading study measured higher pulley forces in the crimp grip (A2 287 N) than in the slope grip (A2 121 N), i.e. roughly 2.4-fold rather than 36-fold.
In that cadaver study, A4 (not A2) rupture was the most frequent event in the crimp position.
In the crimp grip the PIP joint is flexed about 90 degrees and the DIP joint hyperextended; an in-vivo study measured loads up to 116 N over the A2 pulley.
A systematic review states that the full crimp sets the condition for maximum load on the A2/A4 pulleys, and the open hand grip for very low pulley loads.
claims.quote: this sets the condition for maximum loads on the A2/A4-pulleys [8], with forces on the A2 of up to 36 times that of open hand [10]
claims.cited_reference: Larsson ref 8: Schoffl I et al. J Biomech 2009;42:2183-2187; ref 10: Vigouroux L et al. J Biomech 2006;39:2583-2592.

claims.statement: A2 pulley loads in climbing are cited as up to 380 N, rising to about 450 N with sudden shock loading such as a foot slip.
claims.quote: the A2-pulley is regularly exposed to forces of up to 380 N [6], but can reach forces of 450 N if suddenly shock loaded, as for example during a foot slip [7]
claims.cited_reference: Larsson ref 6: Schweizer A. J Hand Surg Br 2000;25:102-107; ref 7: Bollen SR. J Hand Surg Br 1990;15:268-270 (abstracts seen; neither abstract contains these numbers).

claims.statement: Most pulley injuries are said to occur with a sudden sharp increase in finger load, e.g. when a foot suddenly slips.
claims.quote: the majority of pulley injuries occur when a drastic increase in finger grip force occurs, such as when a rock climber suddenly loses foot support [3]
claims.cited_reference: Iruretagoiena 2020 ref 3: Schoffl V et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2003;14 (abstract seen; mechanism not stated in abstract).

claims.statement: In a cadaver study, A2 rupture was the most common failure event under eccentric loading and occurred at lower loads than under concentric loading.
A climbing-medicine review names the crimp grip as the injury mechanism and A2, A3 and A4 as the pulleys at highest risk, especially under eccentric load.
The ring finger is reported as most frequently affected, followed by the middle finger.
claims.quote: The ring finger is most frequently affected, followed by the middle finger (Bollen, 1988).
claims.cited_reference: Bollen SR. Soft tissue injury in extreme rock climbers. Br J Sports Med 1988;22:145-147 (not read).

claims.statement: The A2 pulley is reported as the most frequently affected, followed by A4, often in the fourth (ring) finger.
claims.quote: The A2 pulley is the most frequently affected, followed by the A4, often resulting in damage to the fourth finger [3].
claims.cited_reference: Iruretagoiena 2024 ref 3: Schoffl V et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2015;26:62-67 (abstract seen; it reports MORE A4 than A2 injuries - see notes).

claims.statement: In a 2009-2012 case series, A4 pulley injuries outnumbered A2 pulley injuries.
A scoping review notes one hand-injury study in which A2 pulley injury of the fourth finger was the most common finding.
claims.cited_reference: Vagy ref 10: Bollen SR, Gunson CK. Hand injuries in competition climbers. Br J Sports Med 1990;24:16-18 (not read).

claims.statement: In a recent prospective ultrasound series of 34 climbers, all A2 ruptures were partial and started from the distal edge of the pulley.
In a prospective series of 604 injured climbers (1998-2001, single centre), 20.2% had a pulley-system injury: 48 strains and 74 ruptures.
Study population of that series: 604 injured rock climbers evaluated prospectively January 1998 to December 2001.
Grade distribution in that series: 39% grade 1, 25% grade 2, 30% grade 3, 6% grade 4.
In a later series (836 patients, 911 injuries, 2009-2012), finger injuries were 52% of all injuries and pulley injuries were the most frequent finger injury.
Study population of the 2009-2012 series.
A systematic review summarises pulley-system injuries as 15-20% of all climbing injuries.
claims.quote: Of these, injuries to the flexor pulley system are the most common, and account for 15–20% of total injuries [4].
claims.cited_reference: Larsson ref 4: Schoffl V et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2015;26:62-67 (abstract seen; this percentage is not in the abstract).

claims.statement: Other papers cite a higher figure of up to 33% of all climbing injuries.
claims.quote: Pulley ruptures account for up to 33% of all rock climbing injuries (King and Lien, 2017).
claims.cited_reference: King EA, Lien JR. Hand Clin 2017;33:141-148 (abstract seen; figure not in abstract).

claims.statement: A recent review abstract gives "up to 20%" of all climbing injuries.
A US survey of competitive climbers is cited as finding A2-involving pulley injuries in 26% of climbers.
claims.cited_reference: Berrigan ref 4: Rohrbough JT, Mudge MK, Schilling RC. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2000;32:1369-1372 (not read).

claims.statement: Pulley injuries are described as rare in the general population and seen mostly in rock climbers.
A scoping review of 45 studies found pulley injuries named as the top upper-extremity diagnosis in six studies.
In a prospective adolescent series (137 injuries, 95 patients under 18), only 2 finger pulley injuries were recorded, both sprains.
Acute pulley tears are described as sudden sharp pain during activity, sometimes with an audible pop, followed by finger swelling.
claims.cited_reference: Berrigan ref 3: Crowley TP. J Hand Microsurg 2012;4:25-29 (abstract only seen).

claims.statement: A hand-surgery review describes pain and swelling over the affected pulley and a felt or heard pop at the time of injury.
Reported examination findings are tenderness on the palm side at the level of the injured pulley, swelling and occasionally haematoma.
claims.cited_reference: Simon refs 4 (Miro 2021) and 9 (Climbing Medicine book chapter, 2021).

claims.statement: Symptoms are described as acute focal pain that increases on palpation and on resisted finger flexion, occasionally with inflammatory signs and bruising.
claims.quote: Symptomatology consists of acute focal pain, which increases upon palpation, and counter-resisted finger flexor maneuvers, occasionally accompanied by inflammatory signs and ecchymosis [5].
claims.cited_reference: Iruretagoiena 2020 ref 5: Schoffl V et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2015;26:62-67.

claims.statement: Visible (clinical) bowstringing is described as requiring rupture of more than one pulley.
Bowstringing can be hard to see clinically because pain and swelling mask it and lower-severity injuries show it only subtly.
claims.cited_reference: Berrigan ref 13: Bianchi S et al. J Ultrasound 2007;10:85-92 (not read).

claims.statement: A 2006 systematic review concluded that diagnosing pulley injury by testing for clinical bowstringing is not supported by evidence.
Physical examination is described as non-specific, so imaging is needed to establish grade and number of pulleys involved.
claims.quote: As a physical examination is non-specific, imaging tests are needed to determine the grade of injury and the number and extent of injured pulleys
claims.cited_reference: Iruretagoiena-Urbieta X et al. 2020a (as cited in source).

claims.statement: Chronic pulley injury from repetitive microtrauma is described as focal tenderness and pain while gripping.
Pain and imaging findings do not always coincide: one study had a subgroup with increased tendon-bone distance but no pain on palpation.
claims.quote: Group 3 was composed of 7 rock climbers with a TBD > 2 mm but without pain upon palpation of the injured pulley.

claims.statement: Injured climbers showed reduced one-finger crimp grip strength compared with uninjured controls.
claims.quote: Injured rock climbers presented a decrease in finger grip strength compared to non-injured controls when performing a one finger crimp (p < 0.001).

claims.statement: Grade 1 (as reproduced by Larsson 2022): pulley strain; treatment category conservative (tape).
claims.quote: Pulley strain / Conservative (tape)
claims.cited_reference: Larsson Table 1, "Modified from Schoffl et al. [11] and used with permission" - SECOND-HAND and modified; ref 11 = Schoffl V et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2003;14(2):94-100 (original table not read).

claims.statement: Grade 2 (as reproduced by Larsson 2022): complete rupture of A4 or partial rupture of A2 or A3; conservative (tape).
claims.quote: Complete rupture of A4 or partial rupture of A2 or A3 / Conservative (tape)
claims.cited_reference: Larsson Table 1, "Modified from Schoffl et al. [11] and used with permission" - SECOND-HAND and modified; ref 11 = Schoffl V et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2003;14(2):94-100 (original table not read).

claims.statement: Grade 3 (as reproduced by Larsson 2022): complete rupture of A2 or A3; conservative (thermoplastic ring + tape).
claims.quote: Complete rupture of A2 or A3 / Conservative (thermoplastic ring + tape)
claims.cited_reference: Larsson Table 1, "Modified from Schoffl et al. [11] and used with permission" - SECOND-HAND and modified; ref 11 = Schoffl V et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2003;14(2):94-100 (original table not read).

claims.statement: Grade 4 (as reproduced by Larsson 2022): multiple ruptures, or a single A2/A3 rupture combined with lumbrical muscle or collateral ligament trauma; surgical reconstruction.
claims.quote: Multiple ruptures (as A2/A3, A2/A3/A4) or single rupture (as A2 or A3) combined with lumbricalis muscle or collateral ligament trauma / Surgical reconstruction
claims.cited_reference: Larsson Table 1, "Modified from Schoffl et al. [11] and used with permission" - SECOND-HAND and modified; ref 11 = Schoffl V et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2003;14(2):94-100 (original table not read).

claims.statement: Provenance note for the table above.
claims.quote: Modified from Schöffl et al. [11] and used with permission
claims.cited_reference: Larsson Table 1, "Modified from Schoffl et al. [11] and used with permission" - SECOND-HAND and modified; ref 11 = Schoffl V et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2003;14(2):94-100 (original table not read).

claims.statement: Return-to-sport estimates relayed by Larsson 2022: 6-8 weeks for grades 1-2, 3 months for grade 3; protective taping continued 3 months (grades 1-2) or 6 months (grade 3).
claims.quote: Time to return to sport has been estimated to be six to eight weeks (grade 1–2) and three months (grade 3), with continued use of protective taping for three months (grade 1–2) or six months (grade 3).
claims.cited_reference: Larsson refs 11, 12: Schoffl V et al. 2003 (Wilderness Environ Med) and 2004 (Handchir Mikrochir Plast Chir). Second-hand.

claims.statement: Conservative strategy relayed by Larsson 2022: immobilisation up to 2 weeks (grades 2-3), then functional training with a thermoplastic ring (grade 3) or tape (grades 1-2).
claims.quote: The conservative treatment strategy consists of immobilisation for up to 2 weeks (grade 2–3) followed by functional training and use of a thermoplastic ring (grade 3) or tape (grade 1–2).
claims.cited_reference: Larsson refs 11, 12 (Schoffl et al. 2003, 2004). Second-hand.

claims.statement: The original 2003 paper (abstract) states the management split: grades 1-3 conservative, grade 4 surgical.
The 2006 current-concepts review (abstract) defines grades I-III as strains, partial rupture and single ruptures treated conservatively, and grade IV as multiple ruptures needing surgical repair.
A 2025 narrative review table gives for grade I: light sport activity at 2-6 weeks, full activity after 6 weeks.
claims.cited_reference: Mergoum Table 2 cites its ref 5: Netscher DT, Pham DT, Staines KG. Finger Injuries in Ball Sports. Hand Clin 2017;33:119-139 (not read) - i.e. THIRD-HAND relative to Schoffl.

claims.statement: Same table, grade II: 10-14 days immobilisation, light activity at 6-8 weeks, full activity after 8-10 weeks.
claims.cited_reference: Mergoum Table 2 cites its ref 5: Netscher DT, Pham DT, Staines KG. Finger Injuries in Ball Sports. Hand Clin 2017;33:119-139 (not read) - i.e. THIRD-HAND relative to Schoffl.

claims.statement: Same table, grade III: immobilisation, light activity at 8-12 weeks, full activity after 3 months.
claims.cited_reference: Mergoum Table 2 cites its ref 5: Netscher DT, Pham DT, Staines KG. Finger Injuries in Ball Sports. Hand Clin 2017;33:119-139 (not read) - i.e. THIRD-HAND relative to Schoffl.

claims.statement: Same table, grade IV: operative intervention, return to play around 6 months after surgery.
claims.cited_reference: Mergoum Table 2 cites its ref 5: Netscher DT, Pham DT, Staines KG. Finger Injuries in Ball Sports. Hand Clin 2017;33:119-139 (not read) - i.e. THIRD-HAND relative to Schoffl.

claims.statement: Another paper relays an estimated recovery period of 8-10 weeks for grade 2 (partial A2 rupture).
claims.quote: Partial ruptures of the A2 pulley are graded as a grade 2 lesion and are associated with an estimated recovery time period (RTP) of 8–10 weeks (Lutter et al., 2021).
claims.cited_reference: Lutter C, Tischer T, Schoffl V. Br J Sports Med 2021;55:857-864 (abstract only seen).

claims.statement: ...and 3 months for grade III (isolated complete A2 rupture).
claims.quote: an isolated complete A2 rupture is described as a grade III lesion with an estimated RTP of 3 months (Lutter et al., 2021)
claims.cited_reference: Lutter C, Tischer T, Schoffl V. Br J Sports Med 2021;55:857-864 (abstract only seen).

claims.statement: A newer version of the grading subdivides grade 4 into 4a (double-pulley A2/3 or A3/4) and 4b (triple-pulley A2/3/4).
claims.cited_reference: Simon ref 3: Lutter C, Tischer T, Schoffl VR. Br J Sports Med 2021;55:857-864 (abstract only seen).

claims.statement: In the original cohort, 90-91% of climbers with grade 1-3 injuries returned to sport after three months (as summarised by Larsson 2022).
claims.quote: Schöffl et al. [11, 12] observed a return to sports after three months in 90–91% of rock climbers, with pulley injuries grade 1–3.
claims.cited_reference: Larsson refs 11, 12 (Schoffl et al. 2003, 2004).

claims.statement: In a retrospective series of 47 complete ruptures treated with a pulley-protection splint, 38 of 43 respondents regained their previous level a mean 8.8 months after rupture.
In a follow-up of 21 climbers with grade 2-4 injuries, all regained their climbing level within a year, without a long-term strength deficit.
After surgical reconstruction of multiple-pulley injuries, one centre allows easy climbing after 4 months and full sport-specific load after 6 to 9 months.
One clinic reports having simplified the grading system because complete A2 ruptures and coexistent A3 ruptures were not observed in its series.
Multiple-pulley injuries are described as often needing surgical repair because otherwise contracture and loss of motion and function can follow.
Stated surgical indications at one specialist centre include multiple-pulley injury older than 10 days at start of therapy, or bowstringing that cannot be reduced on ultrasound.
A climbing-medicine review reserves surgery for grade IV injuries not amenable to conservative treatment.
A hand-surgery review states that sequential (multiple) pulley ruptures require surgical reconstruction.
Clinically apparent bowstringing or slower-than-expected healing in grade III injuries is said to possibly require operative treatment.
claims.cited_reference: Mergoum ref 7: Rosenbaum YA, Awan HM. Phys Sportsmed 2017;45:151-158 (not read).

claims.statement: A literature review describes grade 3 as a grey area between conservative and surgical treatment.
A case series of triple-pulley ruptures found that delayed diagnosis and treatment was associated with less favourable results.
That same series suggests early conservative treatment may work even for triple-pulley ruptures, in tension with the "grade 4 = surgery" rule.
Plain radiographs are recommended to rule out fractures when a pulley injury is suspected.
Chronic finger pain in young, intensively training climbers is said to need careful evaluation including radiographs.
Pain on the back (dorsal side) of the PIP joint in adolescent climbers is said to warrant prompt investigation.
Accurate diagnosis is described as a prerequisite for triage because prognosis and treatment depend on the number and severity of injured pulleys.
An imaging review concludes ultrasound should be the primary imaging modality for A2 pulley injuries.
A climbing-medicine review recommends ultrasound first and MRI if ultrasound is inconclusive.
By contrast, a general sports-medicine narrative review calls MRI the gold standard and ultrasound an alternative.
Reported ultrasound sensitivity 0.94-1.00 and specificity 0.94-1.00, based on four studies (two clinical, two cadaveric).
A systematic review found the tendon-to-bone distance used to diagnose complete rupture varied from 1.9 to 5.1 mm for A2 and 1.8 to 3.1 mm for A4.
A 2 mm threshold for complete rupture is described as the most commonly used.
claims.quote: Most researchers have used a 2 mm threshold to diagnose a complete pulley rupture (Miro et al., 2021).
claims.cited_reference: Miro PH et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2021;32:247-258 (abstract only seen).

claims.statement: Klauser 2002 (as tabulated by Berrigan): complete tear >=3 mm, incomplete <3 mm, combined A2+A3 >=5 mm, measured 15-20 mm from the base of the proximal phalanx.
claims.cited_reference: Klauser A et al. Radiology 2002;222:755-761 (abstract seen: it states >1.0 mm was read as positive for a pulley injury).

claims.statement: Klauser 2002 abstract: a tendon-phalanx distance over 1.0 mm was interpreted as positive for pulley injury.
Hauger 2000 cadaver thresholds (as relayed by Berrigan): partial 0-3 mm, complete 2-5 mm, multiple-pulley 5-8 mm.
claims.cited_reference: Berrigan ref 15: Hauger O et al. Radiology 2000;217:201-212 (not read).

claims.statement: A cadaver study found a minimum distance of 1.6 mm for partial rupture and suggests values above 3 mm indicate high-grade partial or complete rupture.
claims.quote: The minimum tendon-to-bone distance value for a partial rupture was 1.6 mm, and tendon-to-bone distance values above 3 mm suggest a high-grade partial pulley rupture (15 mm incision) or a complete pulley rupture.

claims.statement: The same study argues 2 mm cannot by itself identify a complete A2 rupture, since partial ruptures also exceeded it.
claims.quote: Accordingly, we think that this value cannot serve to directly diagnose a complete rupture of the A2 pulley.

claims.statement: Authors state there is no agreement on measurement protocol or reference distance values.
claims.quote: There is currently no agreement on the optimal measurement protocols or specific TBD reference values to diagnose a pulley injury, especially due to the heterogeneity of the anatomical landmark used [18].
claims.cited_reference: Iruretagoiena 2024 ref 18: Iruretagoiena-Urbieta X et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2020;31:498-505 (abstract seen).

claims.statement: Among nine MRI studies, five used a tendon-phalanx distance of >=2 mm as the diagnostic criterion.
claims.section: Methods and Results - Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)

claims.statement: High-resolution probes (>15 MHz) can show the pulleys directly; MRI is described as helpful when the diagnosis is uncertain.
claims.cited_reference: Simon ref 9 (Climbing Medicine book chapter, 2021).

claims.statement: In a splint-treatment series, mean tendon-phalanx distance after A2 rupture fell from 4.4 to 2.3 mm.
Systematic review conclusion on taping: low-to-moderate evidence it might reduce bowstringing; moderate evidence of no effect on strength or muscle activation in uninjured climbers.
claims.quote: Low to moderate evidence suggests that taping might reduce bowstringing of the finger flexor tendons. Moderate evidence suggests that taping has no effect on MVC or muscle activation in uninjured climbers.

claims.statement: For pain, return to sport, pulley shearing force, rupture protection and strength, the evidence was rated very low to low and not considered reliable.
claims.quote: Evidence regarding pain, RTS, shearing forces against A2, pulley ruptures and MVC were all regarded as “very low”, “very low to low” or “low”, and were thus not considered reliable.

claims.statement: The review gives no definite recommendation on tape because of the low level of evidence.
claims.quote: Due to the general low level of evidence, no definite recommendations for treatment using tape can be given, and future research on the possible effects are needed.

claims.statement: Size of the bowstringing effect: 15-22% less with circular or H-tape in two small crossover trials.
claims.quote: Taping with circular tape or H-tape decreased bowstringing by 15–22% compared to no taping (p < 0.05) [6, 15].
claims.section: Results - Effect of finger taping on bowstringing
claims.cited_reference: Larsson refs 6 (Schweizer 2000) and 15 (Schoffl I et al. 2007).

claims.statement: In cadaver hands, tape (circular or H) did not change the force at which the pulley ruptured; certainty very low to low.
claims.quote: There was no difference in maximum force at pulley rupture between circular tape or H-tape and no tape (p > 0.05) [9, 29]. Certainty of this evidence was graded as very low to low.
claims.section: Results - Effect of finger taping on pulley ruptures, in cadaver hands
claims.cited_reference: Larsson refs 9 (Warme & Brooks 2000) and 29 (Tufaro et al., ORS 2016 poster).

claims.statement: Original cadaver study: authors do not support circumferential taping at the finger base as prophylaxis.
Original in-vivo study: circular taping is minimally effective in unloading A2 and probably ineffective in preventing rupture.
Original H-tape study (8 and 12 previously injured climbers): H-tape reduced tendon-bone distance by 16% in the injured finger; other taping methods did not.
No adverse effects of finger taping were reported in the included studies.
claims.quote: No included studies reported any negative outcomes, or other side effects, of finger taping.

claims.statement: The taping review stresses tape is only an adjunct; the main focus is progressive tissue loading through exercise.
claims.quote: Main focus should always be, as with most injuries, progressive tissue loading through exercise therapy [11, 12, 35].
claims.cited_reference: Larsson refs 11, 12 (Schoffl 2003, 2004) and 35 (Schoffl & Schoffl 2006).

claims.statement: A systematic review of overuse-injury prevention found two prospective studies (658 climbers) in which taping did not protect against overuse injury.
claims.quote: Two high-quality prospective trials including a total of 658 climbers showed that taping did not protect against overuse injury risk (18, 28).
claims.cited_reference: Quarmby refs 18 (Auer J et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2021) and 28 (Josephsen G et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2007).

claims.statement: That review says its results cannot support taping as an injury-prevention measure.
claims.quote: Taping is widely adopted in climbing gyms as means to prevent injury, but the results of this review cannot support its use.

claims.statement: Evidence strength as worded by that review: limited evidence that warm-up, stretching and taping are unrelated to injury; repetitive crimp-grip use might be associated with injury.
claims.quote: Limited evidence suggests that warm up/cool downs, stretching, taping and hydration have no relationship with climbing injury, whereas repetitive use of a “crimp grip” and shoe size reduction might be associated with injury.

claims.statement: Load-related risk factors: strong evidence that higher climbing intensity is associated with higher injury risk.
claims.quote: Strong evidence from prospective and cross-sectional studies indicates that increased climbing intensity is associated with an increased risk of injury, whereas the relationship between climbing volume and injury is much less clear.

claims.statement: Previous injury is reported as highly predictive of future climbing injury.
claims.quote: strong prospective evidence suggests that previous injury is highly predictive of sustaining future climbing injuries

claims.statement: Warm-up: this review found no protective effect of warming up or cooling down against overuse injury.
claims.quote: both warming up or cooling down had no protective effect against overuse injuries

claims.statement: Warm-up: a climbing-medicine review nevertheless states warming up is thought to prevent injury.
The biomechanical basis for the warm-up statement: bowstringing distance at the distal A2 edge rose by 0.6 mm (30%) during warm-up in 16 fingers of four subjects.
Observational studies in youth found finger taping associated with higher injury odds; the reviewers attribute this to confounding by indication.
claims.quote: this association likely reflects confounding by indication, where climbers at higher risk (e.g., those with prior pain or higher training loads) are more likely to use tape
claims.cited_reference: Zielinski refs 30 (Woollings KY et al. Br J Sports Med 2015) and 26 (Barrile AM et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2022).

claims.statement: A narrative review on elite climbing notes little evidence so far on effective prevention measures.
First case series (24 young climbers, mean age 14.5): non-traumatic epiphyseal fractures at the dorsal base of the middle phalanx.
These were fatigue (stress) fractures from repetitive load, with no acute injury event.
The authors advise minimising risk by removing intensive power training from the schedules of athletes of this age.
Series of 28 adolescent climbers (mean age 13.7): middle and ring fingers most affected.
Untreated, the injury can damage the growth plate and leave permanent impairment.
The pain location that distinguishes it in the literature is the dorsal (back) side of the PIP joint.
Reported healing times were long: mean 35 weeks to radiological union of a fracture, 24 weeks for a symptomatic sprain.
Prospective adolescent series: growth-plate (periphyseal) stress injury of the fingers was the most frequent injury, 45.3% of all injuries.
These injuries typically present around ages 13-15 during the growth spurt, predominantly in males, mostly in middle and ring fingers.
claims.cited_reference: Schoffl 2025 refs 35, 40, 45, 54, 55 (incl. Schoffl et al. Am J Sports Med 2022; Miro & Schoffl Br J Sports Med 2024).

claims.statement: That series comes from a referral centre and the authors acknowledge selection bias.
A2 pulley rupture is described as the most common injury in skeletally mature climbers but rare in skeletally immature ones.
claims.quote: the A2 pulley rupture is the most common climbing injury in skeletally-mature athletes (i.e., 49%) [11] and is rare in skeletally-immature athletes [14]
claims.cited_reference: Meyers ref 11: Schoffl V et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2015;26:62-67 (abstract seen; 49% not in abstract); ref 14: Schlegel C et al. Sportmed Sporttraumatol 2002;50:7-10 (not read).

claims.statement: Youth climbers themselves misidentify the commonest youth injury: 36% named A2 pulley injury, 15% named growth-plate injury (survey of 267 competitors aged 8-18).
claims.quote: The A2 pulley injury was reported as the most common youth climbing injury by the largest portion of participants, 36%.

claims.statement: The survey authors argue education about growth-plate injury frequency and the scarcity of A2 injuries in youth could improve care.
claims.quote: Education on the prevalence of finger growth plate injuries and the scarcity of A2 pulley injuries in youth climbers can increase diagnostic accuracy, improve care, and reduce long-term complications.

claims.statement: In the 2009-2012 case series, 14 of 20 injured climbers under 15 had an epiphyseal fracture.
These are chronic stress injuries rather than single-event trauma.
claims.quote: These injuries are rarely the result of a single traumatic event; rather, they are considered chronic injuries (stress fractures) cause by the repetitive, often supra-physiologic stress applied to the fingers during climbing (5).
claims.cited_reference: Ref 5: Schoffl I, Schoffl V. Eur J Sports Med 2015;3(1):27-37 (not read).

claims.statement: They are often not visible on plain radiographs.
claims.quote: Diagnosing these injuries in climbers' fingers can be particularly challenging, as they are often not visible on radiographs (9, 10).
claims.cited_reference: Refs 9 (Miro P et al. Skeletal Radiol 2024) and 10 (Schoffl V et al. Am J Sports Med 2022).

claims.statement: Frequent crimp-grip use is reported to raise the risk of these growth-plate injuries; prevention should address it and overall load.
Under-18 climbers are advised to avoid double-dyno campus-board training.
claims.quote: adolescent climbers younger than eighteen years of age are advised to avoid a climbing-specific training technique, known as double dyno campus boarding, which can damage the physis [11]
claims.cited_reference: Attributed in source to the British Mountaineering Council with UIAA MedCom; cited as Meyers ref 11 (Schoffl 2015) - guidance document itself not read.

claims.statement: Scoping review (11 studies, 149 injuries in 98 adolescents, mean age 14): 98% at the PIP joint.
Prevention messages from the adolescent series: less crimp grip, load monitoring, adequate recovery, education.
Taping evidence is weak mainly because of study design and small samples.
claims.quote: The general low certainty of evidence was mainly due to study design (including lack of control groups, lack of randomization and lack of blinding) as well as low sample sizes

claims.statement: Recovery timelines come from uncontrolled cohorts, so natural recovery cannot be excluded as the explanation.
claims.quote: a natural, intervention-independent, recovery process cannot be ruled out

claims.statement: Cadaver findings may not transfer to living, trained climbers.
claims.quote: we should not a priori assume that dead tissue possesses the same properties as living tissue, and especially not living tissue that has been conditioned through years of climbing specific training

claims.statement: Imaging methods vary considerably across studies (positioning, resistance, diagnostic criteria).
A systematic review of ultrasound diagnosis found no consensus diagnostic criteria.
In 2006 a systematic review stated there were no evidence-based published guidelines on diagnosis and treatment.
A 2023 commentary notes a paucity of guidance on rehabilitation and return-to-sport parameters.
A 2025 Delphi protocol states that treatment, rehabilitation and return-to-sport parameters for climbing injuries are poorly documented (consensus not yet published in what was read).
Treatment of pulley ruptures is described as guided mostly by historical methods, small case series and case reports.
How many pulleys must rupture to produce symptomatic bowstringing is described as controversial.
A treatment systematic review could include only four clinical studies.
Prevention-evidence quality is variable and conclusions should be treated with caution.
claims.quote: The methodological quality of the included studies was variable (SQS: 8/32–20/32) and bias is likely to have impacted the findings in several studies.

claims.statement: Epidemiological figures cannot be pooled because of heterogeneity.
The cadaver distance study flags its small sample and dissection artefacts.
claims.quote: The main limitations of the present study are its small sample size and the distortion due to the artifacts produced in the ultrasound images because of prior dissection.

claims.statement: The finding that A2 ruptures are mostly partial needs confirmation in larger samples.
The new growth-plate injury classification has not yet been tested for reliability.
claims.quote: Additional research is required to assess the reliability and reproducibility of this classification system.

claims.statement: Definitive guidelines for adolescent growth-plate stress injuries were described as pending in 2022; the evaluated algorithm is level-4 evidence.
